narrative.headline: Day 1 checkpoint: 1,790 components and 83 findings in juice-shop, with 7 Critical and 29 High issues concentrated in vulnerable npm dependencies and unpinned CI actions; no change baseline is available yet.
narrative.what_is_in_the_app: juice-shop is an npm-heavy application: 1,754 npm packages (155 direct, 1,599 transitive, max depth 9) alongside 25 GitHub Actions, 8 Docker and 3 URL components, spread across 1,114 prod, 646 dev, 28 CI and 2 build scope components. It ships 16 CI workflows plus Dockerfiles and compose files, and references container images including node:24, node:20.19.2 variants, nginx:1.28.0-alpine, redis:7.4.4-alpine, mongo:4.4.29, alpine:latest and a distroless nodejs24 image. The OSV.dev lookup checked these components and found 55 vulnerable components carrying 139 advisories. No untrusted origins or install scripts were recorded in the inventory itself.
narrative.what_changed: No change set was supplied for this run (the packet's what_changed is null), and every listed finding has new_in_change set to false, with counts.new_in_change at 0. So there is no evidence in this packet that anything was introduced by a recent change, and nothing can be attributed to a latest commit or release. The findings should be read as the standing Day 1 baseline rather than a change review.
narrative.what_appears_risky: The stack carries 7 Critical and 29 High findings, led by vulnerable dependency chains: handlebars@4.7.7 with 11 advisories (F-001), sequelize@6.37.3 (F-002), marsdb@0.6.11 (F-005), crypto-js@3.3.0 (F-006) and lodash@2.4.2 (F-007), plus tar@6.2.1 with 12 advisories (F-008). Separately, CI supply chain exposure is real: GITHUB_TOKEN is passed to unpinned third-party actions in ci.yml and image_actions.yml (F-003, F-004), and ci.yml also pipes a downloaded script into a shell (F-017). The triage agent assessed that missing lockfiles next to package.json/ frontend/package.json with range-declared dependencies are suspicious or need human review (F-045, F-049), which would compound the dependency risk if confirmed.

top_concerns.why: Critical: GITHUB_TOKEN is handed to the unpinned coverallsapp/github-action@v2 in ci.yml, and the same action is independently flagged by F-018 for not being SHA-pinned.
Critical: GITHUB_TOKEN is passed to the unpinned calibreapp/image-actions@main, with F-019 flagging the same action for lacking a commit-SHA pin.
Critical at CVSS 9.8 and the widest dependency hit in the packet, with 11 known advisories on handlebars@4.7.7.
Critical CVSS 9.8 on sequelize@6.37.3, a direct dependency rather than a deep transitive one.
High, but the largest advisory count in the packet at 12 known vulnerabilities on tar@6.2.1.

caveats: No change data was provided (what_changed is null), so this is a baseline snapshot and cannot confirm or deny regression from a recent change.
The findings array lists only the top 25 of 83 findings; Medium and Low items and the remaining 58 findings were not available for this summary.
ai_triage output is inference, not evidence: it covers only F-045, F-048 and F-049, and its lockfile verdicts should be confirmed against the repository before being treated as fact.
Vulnerability counts come from the OSV.dev lookup (55 vulnerable components, 139 advisories); specific CVE/GHSA identifiers were not included in the packet and are therefore not cited.

F-045.rationale: F-045/E1 confirms the verified fact: frontend/package.json has no adjacent package-lock.json or yarn.lock and 61 dependencies are declared with ranges, which directly conflicts with the organisation policy requiring a lockfile. However, the packet contains no evidence of an actually compromised or malicious release, no install-script concerns, and no related findings on any component (F-045/T1 reports no graph component, F-045/T2 reports no file location), so the AP-10 scenario of sabotage pulled in through a range remains a mechanism-level risk rather than an observed event. The matched AP-10 indicators are only the unpinned ranges and the missing lockfile; the 'sudden release after a long gap' indicator is not established anywhere in the packet. The innocent explanation that this frontend project resolves versions through a CI-generated lockfile or is not built for production scope is plausible and cannot be excluded from the packet.
benign_explanations: Lockfile is generated in CI or intentionally not committed, so builds are still reproducible
Frontend package.json may be part of a non-production or example application
Ranges are declared by convention while effective versions are pinned elsewhere in the pipeline
F-045.recommended_next_step: Have a reviewer confirm whether a lockfile is produced and enforced in the build pipeline for frontend/package.json, whether this project ships to production, and whether the broad dependency ranges resolve to known-good versions before deciding on pinning or lockfile enforcement.

F-048.rationale: F-048/E1 shows a postinstall that only installs the local frontend workspace and runs the repository's own build targets; F-048/T1 places it directly beside the sibling build:frontend, build:server, cypress and lint scripts, which is the shape of an application's own lifecycle script rather than a dependency payload. Nothing in the script downloads or executes remote code, reads environment variables or credentials, and F-048/T2 and F-048/T3 show no registry component or dependency-graph entry, so the flagged file is the project's own package.json and not a consumed third-party package. This matches the playbook false-positive class of 'the application's own lifecycle scripts that only build or copy local files'. The remaining concern is purely policy-level: install scripts are blocked unless allow-listed, and a build-on-install hook still runs arbitrary build code in CI.
benign_explanations: The application's own postinstall builds the frontend bundle and compiles the server with tsc, i.e. local build steps only
The script sits in a block of ordinary build/test/lint scripts in the repository's root package.json, consistent with normal project tooling
No external binary download, no environment/credential access and no recent introduction (new_in_latest_change is false) point to routine build automation
F-048.recommended_next_step: Confirm with the repository owners that this package.json belongs to our own application source (not an externally consumed package) and, if the project is ever published or installed as a dependency, record a policy exception or move the build out of postinstall.

F-049.rationale: F-049/E1 is a verified fact: there is no package-lock.json / yarn.lock beside package.json while 95 dependencies (including server-side runtime libraries such as express, ethers and @simplewebauthn/server) are declared as ranges, so every install can resolve different code and the organisation's require_lockfile policy is violated. The playbook's false-positive pattern (a library that declares ranges but is always installed from a lockfile) does not apply here, because no lockfile exists at all, which leaves the innocent explanation weaker. The surrounding tools add nothing: F-049/T1 finds no component in the dependency graph, F-049/T2 finds no file location, and F-049/T3 reports no base commit, so the context of this package.json is unconfirmed. Nothing in the packet shows a compromised release, malicious install script or sabotage, so this is a supply-chain hygiene risk rather than demonstrated malicious behaviour.
benign_explanations: The project is a library/skeleton where a lockfile is deliberately not committed and consumers pin versions themselves.
A lockfile may exist but be gitignored or produced only in the CI/build pipeline, so it never appeared next to package.json in the scanned tree.
Dependency versions may be effectively frozen upstream via a private registry proxy despite the ranged declarations.
F-049.recommended_next_step: A human should confirm whether any lockfile is committed elsewhere or generated in CI (check .gitignore and build config), whether this package.json is production runtime scope, and review recent additions to the ranged list - particularly server-side packages such as @simplewebauthn/server and ethers - plus any install scripts, before deciding on pinning/lockfile enforcement.
